questions.q: What measurement probabilities does hand-multiplying the H matrix against |0> actually produce?
questions.explain: H|0> = (1/sqrt2)*[1,1], and squaring each amplitude's magnitude gives 0.5 for both outcomes -- verified directly by matrix-vector multiplication, not just asserted.

questions.q: What do the S and T gates do to measurement probabilities when applied alone to a computational basis state?
options: They double the probability of measuring 1
They change only relative phase, leaving measurement probabilities on the computational basis states unchanged
They always collapse the qubit to |0>
They are only valid inside a function, never an operation
questions.explain: S and T are phase-only gates (quarter-turn and eighth-turn rotations). On their own they don't change measurement probabilities -- a common source of confusion for someone expecting every gate to have a visible effect in isolation.

questions.q: Which of these is equivalent to `CNOT(control, target)`?
options: Controlled X([control], target)
Controlled H([control], target)
Adjoint X(target)
Measure([PauliZ], [target])
questions.explain: CNOT is a convenience operation defined, under the hood, exactly as Controlled X with a single-element control array -- both forms compile to the same underlying controlled gate.

questions.q: In `Ry(theta, q)`, what is the correct parameter order?
options: The qubit first, then the angle
The angle first, then the qubit
Order doesn't matter for rotation gates
Two qubits, no angle parameter
questions.explain: Rotation gates like Rx, Ry, and Rz take the classical angle (a Double) as the first parameter, followed by the qubit being rotated.

questions.q: What is the difference between `M(q)` and `Measure(bases, qubits)`?
options: M only works on functions, Measure only works on operations
M measures a single qubit in the computational basis and returns one Result; Measure is the more general form for joint, multi-qubit measurement in specified Pauli bases
There is no difference; they're aliases
M requires `is Adj + Ctl`, Measure doesn't
questions.explain: M(q) is the common shorthand for computational-basis measurement of a single qubit. Measure(bases, qubits) generalizes this to joint measurements across multiple qubits in specified Pauli bases.
